title: Timeout tests do not prove subprocess cleanup

evidence.quote:
mock_process.kill = MagicMock()
...
patch("asyncio.wait_for", side_effect=asyncio.TimeoutError),
...
assert "timed out" in result.error

patch.object(service, "_get_captions", return_value=None),
patch.object(service, "_transcribe_audio", return_value=audio_result),
...
assert result.source == "audio_transcription"

reasoning: The local transcription timeout test installs a `kill` mock but only asserts the returned error text. A regression that stops killing or draining the child process on timeout would still pass, leaving a production resource leak undetected. The YouTube fallback test also replaces `_transcribe_audio` entirely, so the yt-dlp subprocess timeout/cleanup path has no coverage in these owned tests.
recommendation: Assert `mock_process.kill.assert_called_once()` and that `communicate` is awaited after the timeout. Add a YouTube `_transcribe_audio` timeout test that patches `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec`/`wait_for` and verifies the downloader process is killed and drained.
whyTestsDoNotAlreadyCoverThis: Current assertions validate the user-facing error/source only; they do not assert cleanup side effects on the subprocess mock, and the YouTube test stubs out the subprocess-bearing method.
suggestedRegressionTest: Extend `test_transcribe_local_timeout` with kill/drain assertions and add `test_transcribe_audio_timeout_kills_yt_dlp` for `YouTubeService._transcribe_audio`.
minimumFixScope: Tests for transcription and YouTube subprocess timeout behavior.
